headline: A 2016 federal law widens who can be prosecuted for making or selling certain drugs and chemicals that are likely to be smuggled into the United States.
what_it_does: The law changes the Controlled Substances Import and Export Act. Before, a person had to know or intend that a Schedule I or II drug, a precursor chemical, or flunitrazepam would be illegally imported. Now a person can also be prosecuted if they reasonably believe it will be. The law also bans making or distributing a precursor chemical when the person knows it will be used to make a controlled substance and knows, intends, or reasonably believes that substance will be illegally imported. Separately, it changes criminal code wording from trafficking in a 'counterfeit drug' to trafficking in a 'drug that uses a counterfeit mark.'

who_it_affects.group: People who make or distribute Schedule I or II drugs, precursor chemicals, or flunitrazepam
who_it_affects.how: They can be prosecuted if they reasonably believe the substance will be illegally imported into the United States, not only if they knew or intended it.

who_it_affects.group: People who make or distribute precursor chemicals used to make controlled substances
who_it_affects.how: They can be prosecuted if they know the chemical will be used to make a controlled substance and know, intend, or reasonably believe that substance will be illegally imported.

who_it_affects.group: People who traffic in drugs that carry counterfeit trademarks or markings
who_it_affects.how: The criminal code now refers to drugs that use a counterfeit mark, replacing the older term 'counterfeit drug,' which changes how these cases are described under federal law.
